summary: Defines the symmetric key package content type for CMS. It is independent of transport, and CMS can sign, digest, authenticate, or encrypt it.

plainLanguage.summary: This document defines a format for handing symmetric keys, which are keys shared by two parties rather than a public and a private one, from one system to another. The format is a content type of CMS, the cryptographic message syntax, so it can be signed, digested, authenticated or encrypted in the usual ways. The keys inside it are in the clear unless the sender wraps them.

subtitle: A standard envelope for handing one or more plaintext symmetric keys, plus their metadata, from one party to another.

tldr.problem: Systems that provision symmetric keys, for example into one-time-password devices, need a common, transport-independent format for the keys and for facts about them, such as who issued the key and how long it is valid.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6031 defines a CMS content type, the symmetric key package, that holds a sequence of keys. Package-level and per-key attributes, taken from the PSKC key container model, carry the metadata. The package is DER encoded.
tldr.outcome: The package itself is not protected. It is meant to be wrapped in a CMS type that signs, digests, authenticates or encrypts it.

today: RFC 6031 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2010. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the PSKC model of RFC 6030 and the CMS of RFC 5652.

sections.title: What the Content Type Is For
sections.content:
This document defines the symmetric key format content type. It is transport independent, and the Cryptographic Message Syntax of RFC 5652 can be used to digitally sign, digest, authenticate or encrypt it.

The use cases that motivated the attributes are elaborated in RFC 6030 and are omitted here to avoid duplication. The document also includes ASN.1 definitions of the XML element and attributes defined in RFC 6030, and the key package is defined using the ASN.1 in the X.680, X.681, X.682 and X.683 documents.
sections.plainLanguage: The point is a common format, so that the sender of a key and the receiver of it agree on what the key and its metadata mean, whatever transport carries it.

sections.title: The Structure of a Key Package
sections.content:
The symmetric key package content type is used to transfer one or more plaintext symmetric keys from one party to another. A symmetric key package MAY be encapsulated in one or more CMS protecting content types, and the content type MUST be Distinguished Encoding Rules encoded.

The package is a SEQUENCE with a version field, an optional list of attributes that apply to the whole package, and a sequence of keys. The version identifies the version of the structure, and for this version of the specification the default value, v1, MUST be used. The package attributes are restricted by the SKeyPkgAttributes information object set, and an attribute that appears there MUST NOT also appear in the per-key attributes.

Each key in the sequence is a OneSymmetricKey, with an optional list of attributes that apply to that key and an optional key value encoded as an OCTET STRING. The per-key attributes are restricted by the SKeyAttributes information object set, and an attribute that appears there MUST NOT also appear in the package attributes. Each key MUST include the key attributes, the key value, or both.
sections.plainLanguage: A package holds a version number, some facts that apply to every key in it, and the keys themselves. Each key can carry its own facts. The same fact may not appear in both places, and each key must say something about itself.

sections.title: Package Attributes: The Device and the Module
sections.content:
The attributes defined here assist those using the symmetric key package as part of a Dynamic Symmetric Key Provisioning Protocol with Portable Symmetric Key Container attributes. They fall into three categories: attributes that apply to a key package, attributes that apply to a particular key, and attributes that apply to a key policy. Of the attributes defined, only the Key Identifier and the Algorithm key attributes MUST be included; all the others are OPTIONAL. Like PSKC, the content type supports extensibility, primarily through the definition and inclusion of new attributes, and in some instances through the ASN.1 extensibility mechanism where an attribute holds more than one type. Conversion from XML types to ASN.1 is straightforward: the string type converts to UTF8String, the dateTime type to GeneralizedTime, and the XML integer types to INTEGER or BinaryTime.

The package attributes fall into two collections, device information and cryptographic module information, and all of them are OPTIONAL. The device information attributes, taken together, MUST uniquely identify the device to which the package is provisioned. They are the Manufacturer, which takes its value from either the OATH manufacturer prefixes or the IANA Private Enterprise Number Registry and is prefixed with oath. or iana. accordingly; the Serial Number; the Model; the Issue Number, which distinguishes two devices with the same serial number; the Device Binding, an opaque identifier that allows keys to be bound to a device or a class of devices and that MUST be checked against information given to the user out of band when keys are loaded; the Device Start Date and the Device Expiry Date, which bound the period in which the keys on the device SHOULD be used; and the Device User Id, a distinguished name that is informational only, since no check enforces that only a particular user can use the device.

Usage enforcement of the dates MAY only happen on the validation server, because some devices such as smart cards have no internal clock, so systems SHOULD NOT rely on the device to enforce key usage date restrictions.

The cryptographic module attributes uniquely identify a cryptographic module, which is useful when a device contains more than one. At this time only one attribute is defined, the Cryptographic Module Identifier, which uniquely identifies the module to which the key is being or was provisioned.
sections.plainLanguage: The package can say which device and which cryptographic module the keys are for: maker, serial number, model, issue number, a binding value, start and expiry dates and a user name. Taken together the device details have to identify one device, and the binding value is checked against what the user is told out of band.

sections.title: Key Attributes
sections.content:
The key attributes apply to a specific key. The Key Identifier identifies the key in the context of key provisioning exchanges between two parties, which means that if PSKC is used in several interactions with different containers referring to the same keys, the same KeyId value MUST be used, so that metadata can be updated later without changing the identity of the key. The Algorithm attribute uniquely identifies the PSKC algorithm profile, and RFC 6030 defines two profiles, HOTP and PIN. The Issuer attribute names the entity that issued the key.

The Key Profile Identifier carries a unique identifier used between the sending and receiving parties to establish a set of key attribute values that are not transmitted in the container but agreed out of band, so it stands for a reference to that set. The Key Reference attribute refers to an external key to be used with a key derivation scheme, where no key value is transported and only a reference to the external master key is used, for example a PKCS #11 key label.

The Friendly Name holds a human-readable name for the secret key, as a string with an optional language tag; when the tag is absent, English is used, and the tag MUST be a language tag. The Algorithm Parameters attribute holds parameters that influence the result of the algorithmic computation, for example the response truncation and format in one-time password and challenge/response algorithms. It is a choice of a suite, a challenge format and a response format. The challenge format carries an encoding, which MUST be one of DECIMAL, HEXADECIMAL, ALPHANUMERIC, BASE64 or BINARY; a flag for whether the device checks an appended Luhn check digit, which MUST NOT be present unless the encoding is DECIMAL; and the minimum and maximum size of the challenge the device accepts, counted in digits or characters for the text encodings and in bytes for BASE64 and BINARY. The response format carries an encoding, a length for the response the device generates, and a flag for whether the device appends a Luhn check digit, which is only valid when the encoding is DECIMAL.

The Counter attribute holds the event counter for event-based one-time password algorithms. The Time attribute conveys the time for time-based algorithms, and carries the number of time intervals passed from a start point when the time interval attribute is included, using the BinaryTime syntax. The Time Interval attribute conveys the interval in seconds for time-based algorithms, so a value of 30 means a 30-second interval. The Time Drift attribute holds the device clock drift value, a positive or negative number of time intervals that the validation server has established the device clock drifted by since the last successful authentication.

The Value MAC attribute is a message authentication code generated from the encrypted value in the case where the encryption algorithm does not support integrity checks, since AES-CBC does not provide integrity while AES key wrap with a message length indicator does. It holds the name of the MAC algorithm and the base64-encoded MAC value. The Key User Id attribute names the user the key is associated with, as a distinguished name, and is informational only.
sections.plainLanguage: Each key can carry its own details: which key it is, which algorithm profile uses it, who issued it, a name a person can read, the counter or clock values the algorithm needs, and a MAC that proves the encrypted value was not altered. Only the key identifier and the algorithm are compulsory.

sections.title: Key Policy Attributes
sections.content:
Key policy attributes indicate a policy that can be attached to a key. The Key Start Date and the Key Expiry Date mark the beginning and the end of the key's validity period, both in the canonical representation of the dateTime production, and implementations SHOULD NOT rely on time resolution finer than milliseconds nor generate time instants that specify leap seconds.

The Number of Transactions attribute gives the maximum number of times a key carried in the package can be used, and when it is omitted there is no restriction on the number of uses.

The Key Usage attribute constrains the intended usage of the key, and the recipient MUST enforce it. It is a list of values drawn from OTP, for one-time password generation, CR for challenge and response, Encrypt, Integrity for generating a keyed digest, Verify for checking one, Unlock for the inverse challenge used when a device has been locked by too many wrong PINs, Decrypt, KeyWrap, Unwrap, Derive for use with a key derivation function and Generate for producing a new key from a random number and the previous value of the key.

The PIN Policy attribute allows policy about the PIN usage to be associated with the key. It holds the identifier of the key within the container that contains the PIN protecting the key, the way the PIN is used, which is Local, Prepend, Append or Algorithmic, the maximum number of times the PIN may be entered incorrectly before the key can no longer be used, with reasonable values in the positive integer range of at least 2 and no more than 10, the minimum and maximum length of a PIN that protects the key, and the encoding of the PIN, which MUST be one of DECIMAL, HEXADECIMAL, ALPHANUMERIC, BASE64 or BINARY. If the usage mode is Local, the device MUST enforce the failed attempts, length and encoding restrictions, and otherwise they MUST be enforced on the server side.
sections.plainLanguage: A key can carry rules: when it starts and ends, how many times it may be used, and what it may be used for. A key used only to produce one-time passwords says so, and the receiver has to enforce it. A PIN protecting a key comes with its own rules, such as how many wrong attempts are allowed before the key locks.

sections.title: How the Key Bytes Are Ordered
sections.content:
Two parties receiving the same key as an OCTET STRING must use it in exactly the same way to interoperate, so the document defines a correspondence between the abstract syntax of the key field and the notation in the algorithm standard that defines how the key is used, for the AES algorithm and for Triple DES.

For AES, the key expansion of FIPS 197 uses the input key as an array of bytes indexed from 0. The first octet of the key field SHALL become the key byte labelled index 0, and the succeeding octets SHALL become key bytes in increasing index order. Proper parsing and key load is checked by using the given key octets, 2b 7e 15 16 28 ae d2 a6 ab f7 15 88 09 cf 4f 3c, to generate and match the key expansion test vectors in Appendix A of FIPS 197. Encoded as a DER octet string with tag 04 and length 16, the value is those sixteen octets.

A Triple-DES key consists of three keys for the cryptographic engine, Key1, Key2 and Key3, each of 64 bits with 56 key bits and 8 parity bits, and the three are collectively a key bundle. A bundle may use two or three independent keys, and in the two-key case the same value is used for Key1 and Key3. Each key is expanded into a key schedule by the procedure in Appendix A of SP 800-67, which numbers the bits in the key from 1 to 64 with number 1 the leftmost, or most significant, bit. The first octet of the key field SHALL be bits 1 through 8 of Key1 with bit 1 the most significant bit, the second octet SHALL be bits 9 through 16 of Key1, and so on, so that the trailing octet SHALL be bits 57 through 64 of Key3, or of Key2 for two-key Triple DES. The test bundle is Key1 = 0123456789ABCDEF, Key2 = 23456789ABCDEF01 and Key3 = 456789ABCDEF0123, which encoded as a DER octet string with tag 04 and length 24 gives the value 0123456789ABCDEF 23456789ABCDEF01 456789ABCDEF0123.
sections.plainLanguage: The bytes of the key have to be laid out in the order the algorithm expects, so two systems that receive the same key use it the same way. For AES the octets are simply in order; for Triple DES they are split into three sub-keys, and the test values in the document let an implementer check the split is right.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Implementers of this protocol are strongly encouraged to consider generally accepted principles of secure key management when integrating this capability into an overall security architecture.

The symmetric key package contents are not protected. The content type can be combined with a security protocol to protect the contents of the package. One possibility is to include this content type in place of a PSKC package in DSKPP exchanges, in which case the algorithm requirements are found in those documents. Another possibility is to encapsulate this content type in a CMS protecting content type.
sections.plainLanguage: The package holds keys in the clear. Sending one over an open network means sending the keys in the clear too, so the package has to be wrapped in something that encrypts it, or sent over a protected channel.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: The document uses object identifiers to identify the CMS content type, the ASN.1 version of the PSKC attributes, and the ASN.1 modules found in the appendices. All the object identifiers are registered in an arc delegated by RSADSI to the SMIME Working Group.
sections.plainLanguage: Every new element in this format gets a number from IANA, all in the arc that the S/MIME working group manages.

items.label: Unlock
items.desc: The key must only be used for the inverse challenge that unlocks a device.

items.label: Decrypt
items.desc: The key must only be used for data decryption.

items.label: Key wrap
items.desc: The key must only be used for key wrapping.

items.label: Key unwrap
items.desc: The key must only be used for key unwrapping.

items.label: Derive
items.desc: The key must only be used with a key derivation function.

items.label: Generate
items.desc: The key must only generate a new key from a random number.
